item.description:
Identifying and controlling important neurons in neural machine translation

Paper content

KeyWords

Blackbox NLP, neuron activation, NMT

Goal of the paper

This paper tries to develop a new system to analyse which neurons are the most relevant to NMT, and specific NMT subtasks. They develop a method to rank neurons based on their activation correlation accross pairs of models. Then, they study how important the neurons are (and how valid their metric is) by erasing the best ranked neurons and worst ranked neurons. (Their metric correlates with importance of the neuron for translation). Finally, they study what the neurons are important for: position, token identity. They finally used a Gaussian mixed model to predict tense (from annotated data) based on neuron activation. Controlling selected neurons activation can in some cases lead to change in translation output.

Reflexion

Cool stuff

Cool new metrics:

  • MaxCorr: for a neuron, its highest correlation across models
  • MinCorr: for the most highly correlated neurons, the lowest correlation (trying to find neurons well connected with a lot of neurons)
  • Linear Regression from one model to a neuron, and keep the highest mean squared error: neurons where the information is distributed among lots of neurons in another model
  • SVCCA: PCA dimensions for a pair of models (not clear)

Those metric seem to actually be correlated with neuron importance

An how to guide to study neurons:

  • Is a neuron important?
    • Remove it and see how the translation increases or not
  • What is a neuron useful for?
    • Test its activation on a supervised unrelated task
    • Study the expected conditional variance of neurons activatins conditionned on a property
    • Estimate a Gaussian mixture model for predicting a label and measure its prediction quality (how?)

Conclusion

Cool paper. +++

What woud have been needed

  • What precisely were the tasks used for supervised verification? (used the same data with different annotaitons?)
  • Created datasets on english to a language for 5 languages, and only compared eng-A to eng-A, not eng-A and eng-B (mention they could have done it, not sure what for)
  • Mostly focused on eng-spa in their examples and not that much the other language pairs
  • Only looked at the encoder

Other papers to read

  • Linguistic information on multiple levels : morphological (Belinkov et al., 2017a; Dalvi et al., 2017), syntactic (Shi et al., 2016b), and semantic (Hill et al., 2017)
  • meaningful individual neurons in a few NLP tasks (Karpathy et al., 2015; Radford et al., 2017; Qian et al., 2016a).
  • Much recent work has been concerned with analyzing neural representations of linguistic units, such as word embeddings (K¨ohn, 2015; Qian et al., 2016b), sentence embeddings (Adi et al., 2016; Ganesh et al., 2017; Brunner et al., 2018), and NMT representations at different linguistic levels: morphological (Belinkov et al., 2017a), syntactic (Shi et al., 2016b), and semantic (Hill et al., 2017; Belinkov et al., 2017b). These studies follow a common methodology of evaluating learned representations on external supervision by training classifiers or measuring other kinds of correlations (Belinkov & Glass, 2019). Thus they are limited to the available supervised annotation. In addition, these studies do not typically consider individual dimensions. In contrast, we propose intrinsic unsupervised methods for detecting important neurons based on correlations between independently trained models. A similar approach was used to analyze vision models (Li et al., 2016b), but to the best of our knowledge these ideas were not applied to NMT or other NLP models before. In computer vision, individual neurons were shown to capture meaningful information (Zeiler & Fergus, 2014; Zhou et al., 2016; Bau et al., 2017). Even though some doubts were cast on the importance of individual units (Morcos et al., 2018), recent work stressed their contribution to predicting specific object classes via masking experiments similar to ours (Zhou et al., 2018). A few studies analyzed individual neurons in NLP. For instance, neural language models learn specific neurons that activate on brackets (Karpathy et al., 2015), sentiment (Radford et al., 2017), and length (Qian et al., 2016a). Length-specific neurons were also found in NMT (Shi et al., 2016a), but generally not much work has been devoted to analyzing individual neurons in NMT. We aim to address this gap.

Abstract

Neural machine translation (NMT) models learn representations containing sub-stantial linguistic information. However, it is not clear if such information is fully distributed or if some of it can be attributed to individual neurons.  We develop unsupervised methods for discovering important neurons in NMT models. Our methods rely on the intuition that different models learn similar properties, and do not require any costly external supervision.  We show experimentally that translation quality depends on the discovered neurons, and find that many of them capture common linguistic phenomena. Finally, we show how to control NMT translations in predictable ways, by modifying activations of individual neurons."
